opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to how I think. The work I do, like writing kernels or thinking through an attention variant, isn't really a bunch of independent tasks I can farm out. It's one deep problem where I need to hold the whole picture in my head. If I spin up three or four agents, the bottleneck stops being the model's latency and becomes my attention. I'm context-switching between threads, reviewing diffs I only half remember asking for, and I lose the thread of what I was trying to figure out.

With one instance, it feels more like pair programming. I give it a task, watch what it does, and that tells me something about the problem. Maybe it tried an approach I hadn't considered, or it hit a wall that shows me where the real difficulty is. That back-and-forth is where a lot of the value is for me. It's not just getting code written. It's sharpening my own understanding.

The latency also isn't wasted time. While it's working, I'm thinking about the next step, reading a paper, or sketching out the math. So the wait doesn't feel like dead time the way it might if your job were mostly churning through well-specified tickets.

I'm not against running many in parallel. For things that really are independent, like sweeping over configurations, writing tests, or cleaning up a bunch of separate files, it makes total sense, and I think that's where things are heading as the models get more reliable and you can trust them to run longer without supervision. But for research-y work where correctness is subtle and the hard part is deciding what to do, I'd rather have one really good collaborator and stay in the loop than manage a small team I can't keep track of.

r001.rationale: The response discusses latency as less important than attention and says waiting can be useful, but it does not suggest that users would pay more to reduce latency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I've tried the multi-instance thing, and I keep coming back to just one. Part of it is honestly about where my attention actually is. When I'm working on something like a new kernel or a change to an attention implementation, the hard part isn't typing. The hard part is holding the whole problem in my head: what the memory access pattern looks like, what the numerics are going to do, which edge case is going to bite me. If I have three or four agents going, I'm constantly context-switching, and every switch costs me some of that state. I end up being a worse reviewer of all of them.

The other thing is that I think of the latency as a feature in a weird way. When Claude Code is thinking for thirty seconds, that's thirty seconds where I'm reading the diff it just produced, or I'm thinking about whether the approach is actually right. A lot of my best corrections happen in that gap. If I fill that gap by managing a second instance, I lose it.

And then there's a quality argument. With one instance, I can give it a lot of context and really steer it. I can say, no, don't do it that way, here's why the shared memory layout matters, here's what the hardware is actually doing. That back and forth is where the value is for me. When people spread across many instances, they tend to give each one a shallower spec and then accept whatever comes back, because they don't have the bandwidth to argue with four things at once. For throwaway scripts that's fine. For the kind of code I care about, where a subtle bug shows up as a one percent accuracy drop three weeks later, I'd rather have one conversation I actually understand end to end.

So I'm not saying parallelism is wrong. If you have genuinely independent tasks, sure, fan them out. I just find that for research code, the bottleneck is my own understanding, not the model's throughput. One instance keeps me honest about that.

r001.rationale: The response describes Claude Code’s latency as useful thinking time and explains why the speaker prefers one instance. It does not suggest that users would pay more for lower latency.
